headings.title: Introduction to Pressure Sores
headings.content: A pressure sore, also known as a bed sore, pressure ulcer, or decubitus ulcer, is localized damage to the skin and underlying soft tissue. It usually develops over a bony prominence as a result of pressure, or pressure combined with shear and/or friction. These wounds range in severity from mild skin redness to severe tissue craters that expose muscle and bone. In Nigerian clinical settings, patients with prolonged immobility, such as those recovering from severe strokes, spinal cord injuries, or prolonged surgical procedures, face a high risk of developing these painful and potentially life-threatening lesions.

headings.title: Common Anatomical Pressure Points
headings.content:
When a patient remains in one position for too long, specific bony areas bear the brunt of the body weight. Recognizing these anatomical sites allows nurses to prioritize skin checks.

- **Sacrum and Coccyx**: Most common in patients lying flat on their backs or sitting up in bed.
- **Heels**: Highly vulnerable due to the heavy weight of the foot resting on the mattress.
- **Ischial Tuberosities**: Frequently affected in wheelchair-bound patients.
- **Greater Trochanter**: Vulnerable when patients are positioned on their sides.
- **Occiput**: Common in infants or immobile adults lying supine without head repositioning.

headings.title: Causes and Risk Factors
headings.content:
Pressure sores develop when mechanical forces disrupt cutaneous and subcutaneous blood flow. Ischemia sets in quickly when pressure exceeds normal capillary closing pressure, which is roughly 32 mmHg. 

Several compounding factors accelerate this process:
- **Pressure**: Continuous force compresses local blood vessels, starving tissues of oxygen and nutrients.
- **Friction**: Occurs when skin rubs against bed sheets or rough surfaces, damaging the epidermis.
- **Shear**: Happens when the skeleton slides downward while the skin stays put, stretching and kinking internal blood vessels.
- **Moisture**: Incontinence, sweat, or wound drainage macerates the skin, weakening its natural barrier.
- **Nutrition**: Malnutrition and dehydration impair tissue repair and cellular resilience.

headings.title: Stages and Assessment of Pressure Sores
headings.content:
Clinical staging categorizes pressure ulcers based on the visible depth of tissue destruction. Accurate assessment guides appropriate wound care interventions.

| Stage | Description | Clinical Appearance |ing
|---|---|---|
| Stage 1 | Non-blanchable erythema | Intact skin with redness that does not turn white when pressed |
| Stage 2 | Partial-thickness skin loss | Shallow open ulcer with a red-pink wound bed or a fluid-filled blister |
| Stage 3 | Full-thickness skin loss | Deep crater where subcutaneous fat may be visible, but bone and muscle are not exposed |
| Stage 4 | Full-thickness tissue loss | Extensive destruction with exposed bone, tendon, or muscle |

Unstageable ulcers involve full-thickness tissue loss where the base is obscured by slough or eschar. Deep tissue injury presents as a purple or maroon localized area of discolored intact skin due to damage of underlying soft tissue from pressure and shear.

headings.title: Treatment and Wound Management
headings.content: Managing an established pressure sore requires a multi-faceted approach aimed at relieving pressure, cleansing the wound, removing dead tissue, and preventing infection. Debridement is necessary when necrotic tissue or eschar is present, as dead tissue delays healing and fosters bacterial growth. Nurses use various dressings depending on the wound bed characteristics, choosing moisture-retentive options for clean granulating wounds and absorbent dressings for heavily draining sores. Pain management is integral, particularly during dressing changes. Nutritional support with high protein intake is vital to promote cellular regeneration and collagen synthesis.

headings.title: Prevention Strategies in Nursing Care
headings.content: Prevention remains the gold standard in nursing practice, as managing advanced ulcers consumes extensive resources and causes patient suffering. The cornerstone of prevention is regular repositioning, typically turning bedbound patients every two hours and shifting wheelchair users every hour. Using specialized pressure-relieving mattresses, cushions, and heel protectors helps distribute body weight more evenly. Keeping skin clean and dry protects against moisture-associated skin damage. Routine risk assessment tools, such as the Braden Scale, help nurses identify vulnerable patients early so targeted preventative care can begin immediately upon admission.
